title: Examination of a pigmented skin lesion

guidelineVersions: NICE NG14: Melanoma: assessment and management (published 29 July 2015; last updated January 2024)
NICE QS130: Skin cancer quality standard, quality statement 3: dermoscopy (published 21 September 2016)
NICE NG12: Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (last updated May 2025)

related.why: Excision of a skin lesion, the procedural counterpart
Melanoma: reading the histology report, staging and margins, once a lesion is excised

brief.scenario: Ms Eleanor Rookwood, 49, has a pigmented lesion on her upper back that has changed.
brief.task: Examine the lesion and describe the features that concern you.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Describe the lesion systematically before interpreting it, then decide whether it needs urgent specialist assessment.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: A reassuring 'ABCDE' checklist is not a diagnosis, and nodular melanoma may not fit the classic flat, asymmetric pattern.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Would it be alright if I have a look at the lesion on your back?"

flow: Regional lymph nodes and rest of the skin

grid.label: Consent and exposure
grid.fail: Examines the lesion without introducing himself or gaining consent.
grid.pass: Introduces self, confirms identity, gains consent, offers a chaperone, and exposes the back adequately with good lighting.
grid.high: Explains he will describe what he sees before giving an opinion, and checks she is comfortable throughout.

grid.label: Systematic description
grid.fail: Gives an opinion ('this looks like melanoma') without describing the lesion first.
grid.pass: Describes site, size, colour, symmetry, border and surface in that order before interpreting.
grid.high: Uses precise descriptive terms (for example, irregular, notched border; two or more colours) rather than vague impressions.

grid.label: Features concerning for melanoma
grid.fail: Uses ABCDE as a diagnostic rule and stops there.
grid.pass: Identifies asymmetry, irregular border, multiple colours, diameter change and evolution as concerning features, without treating them as diagnostic.
grid.high: Notes bleeding or crusting as additional concerning features, and that irregularity raises concern without being diagnostic on its own.

grid.label: Atypical presentations
grid.fail: Assumes any melanoma will be a flat, asymmetric, multicoloured lesion.
grid.pass: Recognises nodular melanoma may not follow the classic flat pigmented pattern and can present as a raised, uniform lesion.
grid.high: Actively looks for a rapidly growing, raised, firm nodule as a distinct pattern warranting the same urgency.

grid.label: History and associated examination
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about evolution, symptoms or family history, or skip regional nodes.
grid.pass: Asks about change over time, symptoms, previous melanoma, sun exposure and family history, and examines regional lymph nodes when clinically appropriate.
grid.high: Offers to examine the rest of the skin for other suspicious lesions when appropriate.

grid.label: Dermoscopy and next steps
grid.fail: Says he will perform dermoscopy himself without training, or that a reassuring look excludes melanoma.
grid.pass: States dermoscopy should be performed by a healthcare professional trained in the technique, as part of specialist assessment.
grid.high: Adds that a suspicious lesion should not be reassured from visual appearance alone, and should go to urgent specialist assessment rather than routine review.

grid.label: Presentation and plan
grid.fail: Presents findings without a clear plan or gives a definitive diagnosis from appearance alone.
grid.pass: Presents a structured summary of findings and arranges appropriate urgent specialist assessment rather than reassurance or biopsy in clinic.
grid.high: Explains referral timescale reflects the level of concern and that specialist assessment, not clinic excision, decides management.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello Ms Rookwood, I'm Dr Patel. Would it be alright to look at the lesion on your back? I'll describe what I see before giving you my thoughts, and let me know if you'd like a chaperone.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Inspects.] Upper back, roughly 9mm, asymmetric, an irregular, notched border, two to three colours including a darker area, and a slightly raised surface.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Asymmetry, an irregular border, multiple colours, a change in size, and I'd also ask about bleeding or crusting. Irregularity raises concern but isn't diagnostic on its own.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What if it were a smooth, raised, uniform nodule instead?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd still be concerned. Nodular melanoma is often a rapidly growing, raised, firm, uniformly coloured lump, and needs the same urgency despite not fitting the classic pattern.

high.speaker: candidate

failures.move: Treating the ABCDE features as a diagnostic checklist rather than a prompt for concern.
failures.consequence: A lesion that fails one criterion is wrongly dismissed, or one that meets several is wrongly called melanoma outright.

failures.move: Reassuring because a lesion is smooth, raised and uniformly coloured.
failures.consequence: Nodular melanoma can be missed, since it doesn't follow the classic flat, multicoloured pattern.

failures.move: Performing dermoscopy or an equivalent without training, or treating a naked-eye look as sufficient to reassure.
failures.consequence: Misses features only visible with trained dermoscopic assessment, delaying diagnosis.

failures.move: Biopsying or excising the lesion in this clinic instead of referring.
failures.consequence: Bypasses the specialist pathway that plans margins and further management around a confirmed diagnosis.

recovery.when: You gave a definitive diagnosis from appearance
recovery.line: I should be clearer: these features are concerning, but only specialist assessment, including dermoscopy, can take this further.
I'd also like to examine the nearby lymph nodes before finishing.

knowledge.fact: Describe site, size, colour, symmetry, border, surface and evolution systematically before interpreting a pigmented lesion.
Concerning features: asymmetry, irregular border, multiple colours, change in size, shape or colour, and bleeding or crusting; none is diagnostic alone.
Nodular melanoma may present as a raised, firm, uniformly coloured, rapidly growing lesion rather than the classic flat, multicoloured pattern.
Dermoscopy of a referred pigmented lesion should be performed by a healthcare professional trained in the technique.
Do not reassure a patient about a suspicious pigmented lesion based on visual appearance alone; arrange specialist assessment.

recall.think: Could this be melanoma, including an atypical nodular pattern?
recall.say: "These features are concerning and need urgent specialist assessment."
do: Ask about evolution, symptoms, personal and family history
Examine regional nodes; consider the rest of the skin
recall.trap: A smooth, uniformly coloured, raised lesion is not automatically reassuring, nodular melanoma can look like this.
recall.finish: Urgent specialist assessment with trained dermoscopy; no reassurance or excision from appearance alone in this clinic.

partner.opening: Please examine this lady's pigmented lesion and describe what concerns you. I'll stop you at 6 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Eleanor Rookwood, 49, an office manager. You noticed the mole on your upper back has grown and darkened over the last two months; a relative pointed it out. It isn't painful but occasionally itches. No bleeding. No previous melanoma or skin cancer. Your mother had a melanoma removed in her 60s. You use sunbeds occasionally and had bad sunburn as a teenager on holiday.

reveals.finding: Upper back, roughly 8 to 9mm, asymmetric, irregular notched border, two to three shades of brown, slightly raised in one area.
Grown and darkened over about two months; occasionally itchy; no bleeding.

reveals.trigger: Asks about personal and family history
reveals.finding: No previous melanoma; mother had a melanoma removed in her 60s; occasional sunbed use; bad sunburn as a teenager.
No palpable axillary or other regional lymphadenopathy.

push.question: Is every irregular mole melanoma?
push.expect: No, irregularity increases concern but is not diagnostic.

push.question: Can dermoscopy be done by anyone?
push.expect: It should be performed by a healthcare professional trained in the technique.

push.question: What would you do if you were concerned?
push.expect: Arrange urgent specialist assessment rather than reassure or biopsy in this clinic.

curveballs.prompt: She says a friend told her it's fine because it isn't bleeding.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explains that absence of bleeding doesn't exclude melanoma; the changing size, colour and border are still concerning and warrant assessment.

curveballs.prompt: The lesion is actually a smooth, firm, raised nodule with one uniform dark colour.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Still treats it with the same urgency: nodular melanoma may present exactly this way despite lacking the classic flat, multicoloured pattern.

curveballs.prompt: She asks if you can just remove it today since she's worried.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explains the lesion needs urgent specialist assessment, including trained dermoscopy, before any excision is planned.

curveballs.prompt: She mentions a second, different-looking mole on her arm that has also changed.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Offers to examine the rest of her skin, and includes both lesions in the urgent referral.
